ABSTRACT 40

Objective: Rising cesarean section (CS) rates in low- and middle-income countries may mask a 41

triple burden of unmet need, overuse, and unsafe provision. Using the Robson Ten-Group 42

Classification, a global standard for monitoring and comparing institutional deliveries, we 43

examine CS incidence and associations with adverse outcomes. 44

Methods: Data were drawn from the Pregnancy Risk, Infant Surveillance, and Measurement 45

Alliance Maternal and Newborn Health Study, an open cohort study conducted from 2022 to 46

2025 in Kenya, Zambia, India, and Pakistan. We generated descriptive statistics for Robson 47

Groups and within-group relative risks of adverse events for CS versus vaginal delivery using 48

multivariable adjusted log Poisson models. 49

Results: Among 10,996 women, 29% delivered by CS. Group 5 (prior CS) and Group 10 50

(preterm) were the largest contributors to CS, accounting for 28% and 17% of all CS deliveries, 51

respectively. Between-site differences in CS incidence were most pronounced for Groups 2 and 52

4 (induced labor/pre-labor CS), ranging from 20-60% for nullipara and 7-44% for multipara. 53

Compared to vaginal delivery, CS was associated with increased risk of maternal near-miss, 54

prolonged hospitalization, hemorrhage, and newborn intensive care unit admission. These 55

associations differed in magnitude when stratified by Robson Group, with the greatest risk 56

among lower-risk groups. 57

Conclusion: Repeat CS, preterm deliveries, labor induction, and pre-labor CS were key drivers 58

of CS, with considerable differences between sites. Equipping facilities to safely manage labor 59

induction, trials of labor after cesarean, and preterm deliveries is critical to improving quality of 60

care. 61

INTRODUCTION 62

Background 63

Global cesarean section (CS) rates rose from 7% in 1990 to 21% in 2021, with projections 64

showing a continued rise of 4% annually [1, 2]. In many low- and middle-income countries 65

(LMICs), unmet need for CS persists alongside non-medically indicated or poor quality 66

procedures, imposing a triple burden of underuse, overuse, and unsafe provision that poses 67

risks to patients and strains health systems [3, 4]. Interpreting CS trends is further complicated 68

by the growing prevalence of non-communicable diseases in pregnancy, such as hypertension 69

and diabetes, which contribute to the likelihood of surgical delivery [5, 6]. 70

Though population-level CS rates are used for benchmarking, the World Health Organization 71

(WHO) does not recommend a single target CS rate. Ecological analyses have suggested that 72

population-level CS rates below 9% may reflect underuse, while rates above 15-16% are not 73

associated with reductions in maternal or neonatal mortality after adjustment for socioeconomic 74

factors [7–9]. These thresholds should be interpreted cautiously, as they do not account for 75

differences in case-mix complexity, referral patterns, or maternal risk profiles. 76

The Robson Ten-Group Classification System provides a standardized method for categorizing 77

deliveries into mutually exclusive groups based on parity, prior CS, labor onset, fetal number, 78

gestational age, and fetal presentation (Figure 1) [10]. By stratifying CS rates according to 79

clinically meaningful criteria, the Robson Classification enables the evaluation of practice 80

patterns and trends across facilities and over time [11]. The Robson Classification has been 81

largely utilized in high-income settings, in part due to its reliance on accurate gestational age 82

dating, which remains a challenge in LMICs [4]. 83

Previous research demonstrates significant differences in CS rates by Robson Classification 84

group [12]. Across diverse settings, Group 5 (prior CS) consistently contributes the largest share 85


<!-- Page 5 -->


4

of CS, accounting for 15-50% of CS deliveries and reflecting the domino effect from primary to 86

repeat CS [13]. Groups 1 and 2 (nullipara with spontaneous labor or induced labor/pre-labor CS, 87

respectively) account for 30-50% of CS [14]. Most studies using the Robson Classification focus 88

on group size and contribution to overall CS rate; data linking delivery mode to maternal and 89

neonatal morbidity and mortality within Robson Groups remain sparse. Without these data, 90

interpretation of whether observed CS patterns in LMICs reflect appropriate, unsafe, or 91

insufficient use is limited [15]. 92

Rationale and Objectives 93

Maternal risk profiles are shifting across LMICs, with hypertensive disorders, diabetes, anemia, 94

and obesity shaping demand for surgical delivery, necessitating risk-stratified evaluation to 95

determine appropriate CS use within comparable populations [16, 17]. We calculate CS 96

incidence and relative contribution by Robson Group in Kenya, Zambia, India, and Pakistan. We 97

further explore association between delivery mode and adverse maternal and infant outcomes 98

by Robson Group, offering new insights into obstetric practice in an underrepresented context. 99

MATERIALS AND METHODS 100

Study design and population 101

We use data from the Pregnancy Risk, Infant Surveillance, and Measurement Alliance 102

(PRISMA) Maternal and Newborn Health Study: a prospective cohort study in Kenya, Zambia, 103

Ghana, India, and Pakistan. Study procedures have been described previously [18]. Briefly, 104

study assessments were conducted at <20, 20, 28, 32, and 36 weeks of gestation, at delivery or 105

within three days postpartum, and at one, four, and six weeks, six months, and one year 106

postpartum. Labor and delivery information was collected by trained staff through observation, 107

maternal recall, and/or record abstraction. This analysis included participants with pregnancy 108

duration ≥28 weeks, birthweight ≥1000 grams, institutional delivery, confirmed mode of delivery, 109

and who completed a six-week postpartum follow-up visit. We restricted analysis to participants 110


<!-- Page 6 -->


5

enrolled between 2022 and 2025 and excluded Ghana site data due to missing data at time of 111

analysis. Enrollment began in September 2022 in Pakistan, November 2022 in Kenya, 112

December 2022 in Zambia, July 2023 in South India, and December 2023 in North India. 113

Variable definitions 114

Robson Groups were defined according to the WHO Implementation Manual, based on parity, 115

previous CS, fetal presentation, number of fetuses, gestational age, and labor onset [11]. All 116

participants completed an ultrasound at <20 weeks gestation. Gestational age at delivery was 117

determined by best obstetric estimate, which combines early-pregnancy ultrasound dating and 118

reported date of last menstrual period. Parity and previous CS were self-reported. Labor onset 119

was reported as spontaneous, induced, or pre-labor CS. 120

We included adverse outcomes that occurred between delivery and six weeks postpartum (case 121

definitions in Table S1). Maternal outcomes included prolonged hospitalization, severe 122

postpartum hemorrhage, maternal near-miss, and postpartum depression. Infant adverse 123

outcomes included neonatal death, possible severe bacterial infection, and neonatal intensive 124

care unit (NICU) admission. 125

Statistical analysis 126

Robson group sizes, CS incidence, and the absolute and relative contributions of each group to 127

the overall proportion of CS were calculated for all sites combined and separately, in line with 128

the Robson Classification Implementation Manual [11]. We calculated within-group associations 129

of CS with adverse outcomes using Generalized Linear Models with log link and Poisson 130

distribution and robust standard error, adjusting for maternal age group, educational attainment 131

category, body mass index at enrollment, height, wealth quintile, and study site. Statistical 132

analyses were performed using Stata 18.5 MP-Parallel Edition and R version 4.2.2 software. 133

RESULTS 149

We analyzed data for 2,242 women in Kenya, 1,415 in Zambia, 1,828 in North India, 1,919 in 150

South India, and 3,592 in Pakistan (N=10,996; Figure 2). Table 1 presents a descriptive 151

snapshot of facility-level delivery patterns for one month in 2025 (intended as contextual 152

information). Most women were 20-34 years (84%), completed secondary education or higher 153

(72%), and were multiparous (68%) (Table 2, Table S2). Thirteen percent reported a previous 154

cesarean. Among current pregnancies, 97% were singleton, 96% cephalic, and 85% delivered 155

at term. Provider-initiated delivery varied by site: labor induction prevalence ranged from 17% in 156

Kenya to 47% in South India, and pre-labor CS from 3% in Kenya to 19% in Pakistan. CS 157

incidence was 20% Kenya, 26% in North and South India, 33% in Zambia, and 36% in Pakistan. 158


<!-- Page 8 -->


7

Robson Group sizes for the sample as a whole are presented in Table 3 and for each site in 159

Table S3. Throughout the results, each Robson Group is referenced by its most salient 160

characteristic; definitions are provided in Figure 1. Overall, 32% of women were classified as 161

Group 3 (multipara with spontaneous labor), 16% as Group 1 (nullipara with spontaneous 162

labor), 15% as Group 4 (multipara with induced labor or prelabor CS), and 12% as Group 10 163

(preterm deliveries). Combined, Groups 3 and 4 accounted for 46% of the sample. Relative 164

group size differed between sites, with the greatest difference for Group 3, which constituted 165

49% of the sample in Kenya versus 19% in South India. This was followed by Group 2 size 166

variability, ranging from 4% in Kenya to 27% in South India. 167

We calculated CS incidence by Robson Group overall and for each site (Table 3, Figure 3, 168

Table S4). Group 6 (nullipara with breech pregnancy) had the greatest between-site differences 169

in CS incidence, with the lowest in Kenya (50%) and the other sites falling between 74-100%. 170

This was followed by Group 2 (nullipara with induced labour or pre-labor CS), within which both 171

Indian sites had the lowest CS incidences at 20% and 28%, compared with 46-60% for 172

Pakistan, Zambia, and Kenya. Similarly, for Group 4 (multipara with induced labor or pre-labor 173

CS), Zambia and Kenya reported the highest CS incidence at 44% and 34%, compared to 7% 174

and 10% in North and South India. Relative contributions of each Robson Group to overall CS 175

incidence are visualized in Figure 4. Group 5 (prior CS) was the largest contributor to CS at all 176

sites, followed by Group 4 (multipara with induced labor onset or prelabor CS) in Zambia, 177

Kenya, and South India, and Group 10 (preterm deliveries) in Pakistan and North India. 178

We found an overall association between CS and risk of adverse maternal and infant outcomes 179

within six weeks postpartum (Table S5). Specifically, CS was associated with increased risk of 180

maternal near-miss (RR 2.24 [95% CI 1.90, 2.65]), prolonged hospitalization (RR 2.46 [95% CI 181

2.23, 2.72]), severe postpartum hemorrhage (RR 2.24 [95% CI 1.99, 2.99]), and NICU 182


<!-- Page 9 -->


8

admission (RR 2.70 95% CI 2.35, 3.09]) in multivariable adjusted models. There were 183

insufficient neonatal deaths to produce estimates. 184

CS was associated with at least one adverse maternal outcome within Groups 1, 2, 3, 4, and 10 185

(Figure 5, Table S5). Within Group 1, CS was associated with increased risk of maternal near- 186

miss (RR 1.97 [95% CI 1.16, 3.33]), prolonged hospitalization (RR 4.65 [95% CI 3.55, 6.09]), 187

severe post-partum hemorrhage (RR 1.88 [95% CI 1.01, 3.55]), and NICU admission (RR 2.64 188

[95% CI 1.78, 3.92]). Within Group 4, CS was associated with increased risk of prolonged 189

hospitalization (RR 2.44 [95% CI 1.81, 3.30]), severe postpartum hemorrhage (RR 2.24 [95% CI 190

1.11, 4.55]) and NICU admission (RR 2.50 [95% CI 1.54, 4.04]). Within Group 10, CS was 191

associated with increased risk of maternal near-miss (RR 2.64 [95% CI 1.80, 3.86]), prolonged 192

hospitalization (RR 2.47 [95% CI 1.78, 3.42]), severe postpartum hemorrhage (RR 2.67 [95% CI 193

1.65, 4.31]), and NICU admission (RR 1.47 [95% CI 1.19, 1.84]). 194

Compared to vaginal delivery, CS was associated with lower risk of possible severe bacterial 195

infection in infants within Group 2 (RR 0.26 [95% CI 0.09, 0.68]), Group 3 (RR 0.59 [95% CI 196

0.41, 0.87]), Group 8 (RR 0.11 [95% CI 0.04, 0.31]) and Group 10 (RR 0.40 [95% CI 0.18, 197

0.85]). The overall association between CS and possible severe bacterial infection was 198

insignificant. 199

DISCUSSION 200

We examined CS incidence and within-Robson-Group risks of adverse events associated with 201

CS delivery. CS incidences exceeded WHO Robson Group benchmarks, particularly for Group 202

4 (multipara with induced labor/pre-labor CS), Group 5 (prior CS), and Group 10 (preterm) [11]. 203

There was considerable between-sites variation in group size and group CS incidence within 204

obstetrically similar populations, demonstrating the impact of clinical protocols and facility 205

readiness on CS provision. The magnitude of the association between delivery mode and risk of 206


<!-- Page 10 -->


9

adverse outcomes varied by Robson Group; broadly, CS-associated risk was greater in lower- 207

risk obstetric groups (Groups 1-4) than higher-risk (Groups 6-9). 208

We add to an emerging body of evidence linking CS to increased risk of adverse maternal and 209

infant events and found risk was concentrated in Robson Groups 1-4 (singleton, term 210

pregnancies without prior CS) and Group 10 (preterm) [19, 20]. Several explanations warrant 211

consideration. As most CS deliveries in these groups are likely unplanned, the risk may reflect 212

intrapartum complications (i.e. confounding by indication). Alternatively, the CS-associated 213

morbidity in these groups could point to late hospital presentation or delayed service provision, 214

consistent with the Three Delays model and previous research in LMICs [4, 21–23]. Conversely, 215

CS was associated with reduced risk of infant possible severe bacterial infection in multiple 216

groups: plausible as maternal prophylactic antibiotic administration is standard for CS. No 217

association between CS and adverse events was observed for Group 5 (prior CS), possibly 218

demonstrating the safety of planned CS. By comparison, a systematic review estimated that CS 219

was associated with 1.32 (95% CI 1.01, 1.74) higher odds of maternal adverse outcomes in 220

Group 5 [24]. Future studies may compare within-group associations of CS and adverse 221

outcomes by country, as the relationship between CS and hemorrhage or stillbirth may be more 222

pronounced in African versus non-African LMICs [25]. 223

Our analyses revealed substantial between-site variation in both the proportion of participants 224

undergoing labor induction or pre-labor CS and CS incidence following provider-initiated 225

delivery, potentially indicating the influence of facility-specific labor management protocols on 226

operative delivery. Twenty-nine percent of our sample had labor induced: higher than regional 227

induction estimates of 4% in Africa and 12% in Asia, though it may mirror the challenge of 228

generalizing from single-country reviews and the nature of PRISMA study facilities [26, 27]. 229

Although provider-initiated delivery can reduce maternal and fetal risks, labor induction carries 230

risks and evidence is mixed as to whether it increases likelihood of CS [28, 29]. Our results 231


<!-- Page 11 -->


10

show that induction can be performed successfully, as in the North India site which exhibited the 232

lowest CS incidence among Groups 2 and 4 (nullipara and multipara with induced labor/pre- 233

labor CS). Comparatively, the African sites had two-to-six times greater CS incidence within 234

these groups, possibly reflecting circumstances at lower-resourced facilities that lead to fewer 235

provider-initiated deliveries and higher risk of unsuccessful induction, including inadequate 236

maternal and fetal monitoring and insufficient staff to manage provider-initiated labor [30]. 237

This study benefits from a robust dataset and accurate gestational age dating. To our 238

knowledge, ours is the first publication applying the Robson Classification to facilities in Zambia, 239

and we contribute to a small scholarship from India, Pakistan, and Kenya [31, 32]. As our 240

facilities were not selected randomly, we cannot generalize our findings nationally. Interpretation 241

of results is hindered without information on clinician training and experience level, as well as by 242

the inclusion of facilities that lacked the capacity to carry out CS and those that were referral 243

centers. We were further limited by missing data, with 7% of our sample missing at least one 244

Robson Group criteria and classified as “Unknown.” 245

CONCLUSIONS 246

Our results revealed variation in CS incidence within comparable obstetric populations across 247

four LMICs, most notably for Groups 2 and 4, revealing the importance of facility readiness for 248

labor management in determining delivery mode. We found that CS was associated with 249

increased risk of adverse maternal and newborn outcomes within lower-risk obstetric groups 250

(Robson Groups 1-4) and preterm deliveries (Group 10), but not among higher-risk obstetric 251

groups (Groups 6-9) or prior CS (Group 5). This may be explained by scheduled versus 252

unplanned CS, or late CS due to delays in care-seeking or service provision. Our work 253

emphasizes the value of going beyond overall CS rate to better understand context-specific 254

drivers of CS and areas for quality improvement. 255
